payload.body: Sound is a mechanical wave: a propagating oscillation of pressure and particle displacement in an elastic medium (gas, liquid, or solid), and the human category that names and measures it. Parameters: (1) frequency - oscillations per unit time, its reciprocal the period, bounding perceived pitch and the audible band (roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz for human hearing); (2) amplitude and waveform - the pressure deviation from equilibrium and its shape over time (sine, pulse, noise), bounding loudness and timbre; (3) medium - the material carrying the wave, which fixes propagation speed (about 343 m/s in air at 20C) and requires that a vacuum carries no sound; (4) duration and wavefront - how long the oscillation is sustained and how its surface spreads (plane, spherical, focused). Persistence: wave propagation is self-sustaining - each portion of the medium drives its neighbor - so a sound event endures until its energy is absorbed; as a human category sound persists through measurement (microphones, oscilloscopes, acoustic instruments), recording (grooves, magnetic tape, digital samples), and musical and engineering practice that names, compares, and reproduces particular sounds. [formal: sonus | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Rhythm is the pattern of recurrence in time: an ordered sequence of events or states in which the intervals between recurrences, and often their intensities, repeat with a stable period or a patterned variation. Parameters: (1) period or beat interval - the gap between successive events, whether constant (metronome tick, cardiac cycle) or patterned (syncopation, verse meter); (2) accent or intensity structure - which recurrences are marked (strong beat, stress) and which unmarked, what separates a rhythm from bare periodicity; (3) domain of events - the kind of thing that recurs: auditory beats, visual pulses, motor cycles, cardiac and circadian cycles, metrical feet; (4) regularity - the tolerated deviation from exact periodicity, below which the pattern is felt as rhythm and above which it dissolves into noise or chance. Persistence: rhythmic structure endures in embodied oscillators (heartbeat, breathing, circadian systems, metronomes, drum machines) and in the practices that reproduce it across time and people - musical notation, meter, timekeeping, choreography, and the teaching of music, dance, and liturgy. payload.body: A converter is a purpose-built device — a hardware circuit, integrated chip, or firmware/software artifact — whose sole function is transforming a signal or quantity from one representational domain to another while preserving the carried information content across the transfer. Parameters: (1) input domain — the representational form of the incoming signal (e.g., continuous-time analog voltage, discrete digital codes, a given sampling rate); (2) output domain — the representational form produced (e.g., discrete digital codes, continuous-time analog voltage, a different sampling rate); (3) transfer law — the reproducible mapping relating input to output (sampling plus quantization, a quantization ladder plus reconstruction filter, a resampling kernel with interpolation and anti-imaging/anti-aliasing filtering, level or impedance transformation); (4) fidelity constraints — the bounds within which content is preserved (bandwidth, bit depth, jitter, error bound). Persistence mechanism: fabricated as silicon circuits or packaged as firmware and software libraries, distributed through electronics and software supply chains, maintained by the engineering discipline of signal processing, and replaced when the transfer law or fidelity target changes.
